doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: No label pressure at Sony and being a banjo player on a major
summary: Fleck is surprised Sony has not pressured them despite modest sales. He found it cool to be an esoteric group on a major label, like Earl Scruggs before him.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Do you get pressure from your record companies to, “Gee, if you guys could just sing” or, “if you could write another song like that.”

I don’t understand why I’m not getting that pressure. I mean we’re on SONY, they’re spending this big money. Our sales haven’t been that great. They have not put the phone down. Maybe it’s because we’re near the end of the deal and they want to re-sign us, I don’t know. But no, I’ve been very surprised, honestly. I don’t understand it, because I don’t think our records are making money for them but I think we’re probably the best seller they have right now on their jazz roster so maybe — I don’t know what it is. I mean the people keep shifting at the labels too. You know there’s been a lot of firings, there’s all kinds of stuff. But it always seems like we should be on a major label. I thought that was cool. But now in a time when most people think it’s not cool to be on a major label as a banjo player, being on the major label, I mean there was only one other one that ever was for the longest time and that was Earl Scruggs. So to me I thought it was cool to be such an esoteric group, but making it on the majors. And maybe that time is going to pass but I still always thought it was kind of cool to be on it.
